title: Rachel dies on the road (Genesis 35:16–20)
hookLine: she dies bearing Benjamin and is buried by the roadside; tradition says she still weeps for her children

lines: THE ONE JACOB LOVED AT THE WELL.
A HARD LABOR ON THE ROAD.
cards: The family is traveling south, toward Bethlehem, and Rachel is pregnant again. Rachel: the one Jacob loved at first sight by the well, and worked seven years for, then seven more.
She waited years for a child, at last had Joseph, and named him with a hope: may God add another son. Now the hope is coming true. And the labor is hard.
Very hard. The midwife tries to comfort her: don't be afraid, this one is a son too.

teach.h: SON OF MY SORROW, SON OF THE RIGHT HAND.
teach.b: As she is dying, Rachel names the baby Ben-oni: son of my sorrow. Jacob gives him another name: Binyamin, Benjamin, son of the right hand. One name remembers the pain; the other chooses strength.
Then the Torah says, simply: "And Rachel died, and was buried in the way to Ephrath—the same is Beth-lehem." In the way.
Not in the family tomb at Hebron, where Abraham and Sarah lie, where Leah will lie, where Jacob himself will be buried.
Rachel is buried beside the road, and Jacob sets up a pillar on her grave. Why there?

Centuries later, the prophet Jeremiah hears a sound on that road, as the people are being led away into exile: "Rachel weeping for her children." She refuses to be comforted, the verse says, because her children are gone.
And God answers her: refrain your voice from weeping; your children will come back. The rabbis put these together.

Rashi, the great medieval commentator, passes on a midrash: Jacob buried Rachel by the road on purpose, so that when her children were driven into exile along it, she would be there to cry for them, and her crying would be heard.
Rachel became the mother who never stops praying for her kids. And not only in books.
Her tomb, near Bethlehem, is still visited today.
People pray there, especially people longing for a child, or worried about one. A woman who waited so long to be a mother became, in Jewish memory, the mother of everyone far from home.

how: Many Jews visit Rachel's Tomb near Bethlehem to pray, especially for children and for the health of family, and Jeremiah's words about Rachel weeping are read in synagogue on the second day of Rosh Hashanah.

games.q: you're Jacob. Rachel has died on the road, far from the family tomb at Hebron. what do you do?
o: bury her by the road and set up a pillar.
stop the journey and settle there.
games.why: he buries her in the way to Ephrath and sets a pillar on her grave. a midrash says it was so she could weep for her children when they passed into exile.

practice: Let one mother come to mind, yours or someone else's, living or gone, easy or complicated, and picture her face.

Think of one thing she carried for someone else, maybe without anyone noticing, or of a mother you know who is worried about a child right now, and hold her there gently. If you pray, you can pray for her.

wordCard.voice: Ben-oni, the name Rachel gave her second son: son of my sorrow. Rachel dies giving birth to Benjamin, and is buried where her children would one day pass, still weeping for them.

orig.note: Hebrew: Rachel. the name means ewe, a mother sheep.
